suite_baseline.reconciliation: As recorded in parity/control-plane.ledger.json: 2194 collected + 5 modules skipped at collection time = 2199. Unchanged by this belt.

subsystem.name: messagebus
subsystem.note: The S8 durable-messaging belt, interlock tests/messagebus, 5 files. One ledger per source file (D-0019). The belt's whole design constraint is that it adds NO delivery store: interlock's own bus.py opens by defining itself as a thin facade that uses the S7 outbox API as found, so send / recipient-filtered poll / ack / envelope / endpoint is the entire owned surface and retry counting, delivery state transitions, lease fencing, destination dedup and ack persistence all stay in src/control_plane/outbox.ts. The single xfailed case in the whole 2,199-case source baseline lives in this belt (tests/messagebus/test_carried_specifications.py's recipient-aliasing specification).

file.note: Two layers on purpose: the in-process cases drive `Endpoint.handle` directly so every JSON-RPC branch is reachable without process management, and the last two put an actual wire under the claim. The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order. Measured 2026-08-29 against the shared read-only clone of interlock at 65f36c5, `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q tests/messagebus/ -p no:cacheprovider`: 42 passed, 1 xfailed.

systematic_mappings.from: `bus.send(message_id=..., recipient=..., payload=..., dedup_key=..., now_ms=..., epoch=..., run_id=...)`, `bus.poll(recipient, now_ms=..., epoch=..., clock=...)`, `bus.ack(message_id, now_ms=..., recipient=...)` -- Python keyword arguments in snake_case
systematic_mappings.to: the same three verbs taking a single options object in camelCase: `send({messageId, recipient, payload, dedupKey, nowMs, epoch, runId})`, `poll(recipient, {nowMs, epoch, clock})`, `ack(messageId, {nowMs, recipient})`
systematic_mappings.why: The shape `src/control_plane/outbox.ts` already established for the same arguments, so the facade and the module it fronts are called the same way. JavaScript has no keyword arguments; an options object is the repository's settled substitute, and matching the outbox matters more here than anywhere because this class exists to be a thin skin over it. Systematic and therefore not repeated per case.
systematic_mappings.affects: every case that drives the bus

systematic_mappings.from: `@dataclass(frozen=True) DeliveredEnvelope` with snake_case fields, and `dataclasses.asdict(envelope)` at the wire
systematic_mappings.to: a frozen class with camelCase fields, and an explicit `envelopeToWire` in `endpoint.ts` that spells the snake_case wire keys out
systematic_mappings.why: The TypeScript surface is camelCase like the rest of the port, but the WIRE is not the API: `message_id` is the argument name the `ack` tool's own `inputSchema` declares, and an MCP client configured against interlock already parses those keys. So the rename stops at the transport boundary, and it is written out at that boundary rather than falling out of a serializer -- a serializer would make the wire contract a side effect of a naming convention.
systematic_mappings.affects: the envelope and the endpoint's two tool payloads

systematic_mappings.from: `pytest.raises(ValueError)` -- Python spells both the outbox's usage errors and the bus's own recipient-boundary refusal as the one builtin
systematic_mappings.to: `expectRefusal(..., OutboxUsageError)` for the outbox's, and `expectRefusal(..., MessageBusUsageError)` for the bus's own
systematic_mappings.why: `docs/test-translation-conventions.md` records why `expectRefusal` asserts the class as well as the message: a refusal family whose members differ only by message stays green while the taxonomy a caller acts on is wrong. Python collapses these two into `ValueError` because that is the builtin available; keeping them collapsed here would mean an ack refused by the WRONG layer still passed the test. The outbox's own refusals keep reaching callers unchanged, which is the source's stated 'exceptions are the outbox's own' doctrine.
systematic_mappings.affects: the two ack-refusal cases and the endpoint's tool-error case

systematic_mappings.from: `python -m claude_org_runtime.messagebus.endpoint` as the child, reached through `PYTHONPATH`
systematic_mappings.to: `node dist/messagebus/endpoint.js` as the child, with an `isEntryPoint()` guard in the module
systematic_mappings.why: A TypeScript module has no `-m`, and the module a worker's MCP configuration launches is the built one. The guard is `src/cli.ts`'s, `realpathSync` on both sides for the reason recorded there: a symlinked launcher makes the URL form disagree with `process.argv[1]`.

systematic_mappings.from: `json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=True)` for every line the server writes
systematic_mappings.why: `JSON.stringify` does not escape non-ASCII, and the endpoint's own docstring calls its framing ASCII-safe -- which is also `docs/cli-output-policy.md`'s rule for anything that can reach a cp932 console. Rather than write a fourth JSON renderer (D-0017 rule 4: one renderer), the endpoint uses the transcription the control plane already carries. It sorts object keys, which the source's call does not; JSON object key order carries no meaning and every consumer here parses rather than compares text.

systematic_mappings.from: `for raw in stdin` over `sys.stdin.buffer`, decoding each line with `raw.decode('utf-8')` inside a `try`
systematic_mappings.to: a `data`/`end` listener pair over the raw byte stream, splitting on `0x0a` and decoding each line with `new TextDecoder('utf-8', {fatal: true})`
systematic_mappings.why: Bytes rather than a decoded stream, deliberately: Node's default decoding turns invalid UTF-8 into replacement characters, so the -32700 `line is not UTF-8` branch would become unreachable and a client that mangled its encoding would get silence. The trailing partial line is handled on `end`, as Python's iteration handles it.

ids: test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > target-only -- the epoch env value is `int()`, not `Number()`
test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > a database that does not exist refuses to start
test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > a spike database refuses to start
test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > a production database behind migration head refuses to start
target_only_tests.why: The source reads the lease epoch with `int(env.get(...))` inside a `try`, so Python's integer grammar IS its validation and no source case drives a malformed epoch -- there is nothing to translate. This port had to write that grammar out, and the epoch is a FENCING TOKEN: a spelling `int()` refuses but a hand-written parser accepts would start an endpoint whose writes are fenced under a number nobody wrote, where `missing()` should have refused to start at all. The case pins the refusals (`_1`, `1_`, `1__0`, a float spelling, a hex spelling, `1e3`) as well as the acceptances (surrounding whitespace, a sign, `1_000`), and asserts each refusal reaches `missing()`. Target-only because it defends what the port had to invent, not a property of the source.
target_only_tests.note: Three cases, none of them ported coverage, added beside the epoch-grammar case already declared here (the `why` above still stands for that one, unchanged). They pin ONE claim: the endpoint refuses at startup -- exit status 2 and a `FATAL:` line on stderr -- a database it must not serve, in each of the three wrong shapes it can be handed: absent, spike, or behind migration head. NO SOURCE COUNTERPART EXISTS, and not because interlock's suite is thin. interlock's endpoint has one schema and therefore nothing to refuse: it opened the spike control plane, which CREATES the file if it is not there (throwaway by default under interlock D-0026) and asks nothing about what it found, so "which database am I attached to" was a question with no wrong answers to exercise. The refusals are a consequence of THIS repository's spike/production split -- D-0050 (the production schema is the control plane the lap runs on, and the spike schema is not a fallback) and D-0029 (opening never migrates) -- reaching the endpoint, which now opens `openProductionControlPlane` (`src/messagebus/endpoint.ts:10`, `:528`). That opener never creates and never migrates, so it raises `MissingStateRefused`, `CorruptStateRefused` (a spike database, recognised by its `application_id`, for which no migration exists and none will be written) and the base `ControlPlaneRefusal` for behind-head; the three cases are those three raises seen from outside the process. What is at stake is not tidiness: the old opener would have created an empty spike file and served it, giving an endpoint that starts, polls forever and reports nothing wrong while the run's real outbox sits in a file nobody opened -- the failure this belt is least able to notice from the inside, since every observation it could make would be made against the wrong database. The spike case is also the one that could not merely be cosmetic: the spike schema has no `cancelled` outbox status and no gate tables, so an endpoint served from one could never see a gate closure and would deliver relays whose human gate had already closed. WHY EXIT 2 RATHER THAN 1: 2 is the code `endpoint.ts` already uses for missing env (`:523`) and for a recipient no handler serves (`:566`), and a misconfigured database belongs in that family. Left uncaught, the refusal reached the entry-point handler at `:610`, which prints an uncaught FATAL and sets 1 -- the status for "this program crashed" -- so a database nobody prepared would be indistinguishable, to an operator and to any supervisor scripting a restart, from a bug in the endpoint. `expectRefusedStartup` (`test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts:179`) asserts the status and the `FATAL:` line together, and each case runs the real child process rather than calling `main()` in process, because an exit status only exists for a process. Recorded here because it is evidence and not merely tidy: the two pre-existing subprocess cases in this file (`an unregistered recipient refuses to start` and `the acceptance sequence end to end over stdio`) were NOT edited. They pass unchanged against the production fixture, which is what says the re-point preserved the behaviour the ledger's ported entries claim rather than moving it.

entries.reason: Same assertion -- a refusal comes back as a tool-level error carrying the exception's class name and message, the transport stays up, and an unknown tool is a -32602 rather than an isError. Adapted in one word: the text the source looks for is `ValueError`, because that is what its outbox raises for an ack of an undelivered message; continuo's outbox names that refusal `OutboxUsageError`, so the case asserts the class continuo actually has. The rendering itself is unchanged -- `${constructor.name}: ${message}` is the source's `f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"`, read off the constructor rather than `error.name` because an Error subclass that does not set `name` inherits `"Error"` and the whole point of the text is to say which refusal this was.

entries.target_id: test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > an unregistered recipient refuses to start
entries.reason: Same case: a real child process on a real wire, driven over line-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio. Adapted because the child is a different thing. The source runs `python -m claude_org_runtime.messagebus.endpoint` with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at its own `src/`; there is no `-m` for a TypeScript module, and running the `.ts` source would need a loader the shipped package does not have. The child here is `node dist/messagebus/endpoint.js` -- the BUILT module, which is what a worker's MCP configuration would actually launch, and the same choice `test/measurement/cli.test.ts` makes for `dist/cli.js`. `npm run pretest` builds it and the case asserts its presence with a message that says so, rather than failing obscurely. The assertion is unchanged: exit status 2 and `no registered handler` on stderr.

entries.target_id: test/messagebus/endpoint.test.ts::the worker-outbound MCP endpoint > the acceptance sequence end to end over stdio
entries.reason: Same case: a real child process on a real wire, driven over line-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio. Adapted because the child is a different thing. The source runs `python -m claude_org_runtime.messagebus.endpoint` with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at its own `src/`; there is no `-m` for a TypeScript module, and running the `.ts` source would need a loader the shipped package does not have. The child here is `node dist/messagebus/endpoint.js` -- the BUILT module, which is what a worker's MCP configuration would actually launch, and the same choice `test/measurement/cli.test.ts` makes for `dist/cli.js`. `npm run pretest` builds it and the case asserts its presence with a message that says so, rather than failing obscurely. A second adaptation is in the client: `process.stdout.readline()` blocks in Python, and Node's stdio is event-driven, so the test client buffers lines and hands back a promise. The source's `assert line, "endpoint closed stdout unexpectedly"` becomes a rejection wired to the child's `close` event -- without it a child that died would leave the read pending until the file's timeout, reporting a timeout instead of the death that caused it. Everything asserted is the source's, in the source's order, plus one addition: the child's exit status is awaited and asserted 0, because a serve loop that ends by throwing would otherwise leave every assertion above still true.
